title: Tracker Survey 2025: How Consumers Are Choosing Legal Services
author: Legal Services Consumer Panel

dom.t: Solicitor entry: Diverse routes yield unequal attainment

st.t: Solicitor entry: Diverse routes yield unequal attainment
st.an: The source does not address solicitor-entry routes, examination attainment or apprenticeships. It only provides an ethnicity table whose missing headings prevent reliable interpretation, so it cannot establish the cluster’s principal proposition, though it is consistent with the cluster’s caution about this extract.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source examines consumer confidence and provider-selection criteria, especially regulated status, reputation, price, specialism and speed. It provides no evidence about legal AI’s task-level capabilities, verification needs, selective deployment or operating-model redesign, so its position on the cluster proposition cannot be determined.

mo.t: Reliable delivery: Legal engineering bridges capability and service

kp.k: Survey documents consumer experiences, not AI-driven changes
kp.d: The report presents evidence on legal-services choice in England and Wales, without discussing AI or attributing market changes to it. LSCP commissioned M·E·L Research to survey 3,750 people who had used legal services in the preceding two years. Fieldwork ran from 20 February to 7 April 2025 using an online panel with quotas; the sample was weighted by legal service used. Subgroup differences highlighted in the text are statistically significant at a 95% confidence level unless otherwise indicated.
qs: This year we talked to 3,750 legal services users.
Respondents were sourced via an online panel, with quotas set to generate representative results.
The survey was live from Thursday, 20 February to Monday, 7 April 2025.
The sample was weighted to the type of legal service used in the past two years

kp.k: Shopping around increased, with limits on historical comparability
kp.d: The proportion shopping around increased from 41% in 2024 to 44% in 2025, which the report describes as its highest recorded level. However, question wording changed from 2023, making earlier shopping-around data not directly comparable. The research provider also changed in 2022, introducing some methodological changes. A 500-respondent Wales boost in 2025, compared with 250 previously, was downweighted in overall analysis to maintain comparability.
qs: The proportion of consumers who shopped around before choosing a legal services provider has increased in the last year (see Figure 1 - 41% in 2024, 44% in 2025), and is now at its highest level.
*Question wording was changed from 2023 onwards, so data from previous years is not directly comparable.
The 2025 survey includes a boost of 500 respondents in Wales (as opposed to 250 in previous years), to enable robust analysis of legal services users within Wales.

kp.k: Shopping behaviour varies substantially by consumers and legal needs
kp.d: Shopping around was more common among London residents (60%), people aged 25–34 (61%), minority ethnic communities (57%, versus 38% of White communities), and legal aid users (61%). It was also higher among social grades ABC1 (50%) than C2DE (40%). By service, family matters and tenant housing problems showed greater shopping around than criminal charges, patents or powers of attorney. These are reported subgroup associations, not causal explanations.
qs: Those from minority ethnic communities (57% vs. 38% of those from White communities);
Legal aid users (61% vs. 44% overall).

Unsurprisingly, shopping around is higher for more complex legal needs, such as family matters (54%) and housing problems as a tenant (53%). Shopping around is lower for legal services to deal with criminal charges (22%), patents (31%) or a power of attorney (33%).

kp.k: Information accessibility improved, but ethnic disparities persisted
kp.d: Consumers shopping around reported improved ease of finding information about costs, ombudsman access, service duration and professional indemnity insurance. Expertise and cost information were easiest to find, while other information categories remained fairly stable. Respondents from minority ethnic communities reported greater difficulty across most service information categories.
qs: This year, consumers have found it easier to find information on costs, whether they could complain to an ombudsman, how long the service would take, and details of professional indemnity cover (see Figure 2).
Other areas have remained fairly stable, with information on expertise and costs seen as most easy to find.
Those from minority ethnic communities found it more difficult to find information across most aspects of the service when shopping around.

kp.k: Price leads comparisons; quality assurances gained attention
kp.d: Among consumers shopping around, price (56%), reputation (48%) and office location (31%) were leading comparison dimensions, broadly consistent with recent years. Independent verification of service quality rose to 27%, from 22% in 2024, and ombudsman access rose to 15%, from 10%. Here verification means independent assurance of service quality, not checking AI output. Older consumers prioritised price and location, while younger consumers focused more on speed and online service.
qs: The price (56%) of the service was the main aspect that people compared when shopping around, with reputation (48%) and the location of an office (31%) also important factors; all of these were in line with scores seen in recent years (see Figure 3).
The proportion of consumers comparing independent verification of the quality of service (27%) and access to an ombudsman (15%) have increased this year.
Over 55s were more likely than other age groups to compare price and office locations, whereas younger consumers focused more on speed and online service;

kp.k: Perceived provider choice increased but remained uneven
kp.d: Some 84% felt they had a choice of provider in 2025, compared with 82% in 2024. This reached 88% among those shopping around and those satisfied with their legal outcome; the report describes the latter relationship as a correlation. Perceived choice was higher among self-funders (86%) than insurance users (80%) or those using no-win-no-fee arrangements (79%), and lower in Wales (77%).
qs: Over eight in ten consumers (84%) felt that they had a choice, a slight increase on 2024 (82%), and remaining well ahead of levels seen between 2012 and 2021 (see Figure 4).

Those who were satisfied with the outcome of their legal matter were also more likely to feel that they had a choice than the overall sample (88%), suggesting a correlation between overall satisfaction and satisfaction with other areas of the experience.
Consumers in Wales were less likely to feel that they had a choice (77% vs. 84% overall).

kp.k: Prior experience and personal recommendations dominate provider selection
kp.d: Previous use by the consumer or a family member (19%) and recommendations from family or friends (18%) remained the most common selection routes. Recommendations did not eliminate further research: 57% of recipients sought additional information before contacting the provider. Previous-use selection was more common among older consumers (28% for those aged 55+), White consumers (23%, versus 12% among minority ethnic communities), and consumers in Wales (27%).
qs: When asked how consumers choose their provider, influence from family members and friends (they or a family member have used the provider before - 19% or family or friends recommended the provider - 18%) remained the most common factors, consistent with previous years (see Figure 5, overleaf).
Yet the majority (57%) of consumers who received a recommendation still looked for additional information about the provider prior to contacting them.
White consumers were twice as likely as those from minority ethnic communities to use providers they/ their family previously used (23% vs. 12%);

kp.k: Regulation ranked highest among stated provider-choice factors
kp.d: Provider regulation was introduced as a factor for the first time in 2025 and rated important by 89%, making it the highest-ranked factor. Reputation, price, specialism and speed remained important. Regulation mattered particularly to those aged over 55 (92%) and power-of-attorney users (93%). The executive summary frames this as what consumers would consider if they could shop around, whereas the main text and Figure 7 frame it as importance when choosing their provider.
qs: For the first time in 2025, consumers were asked about how important a provider being regulated was in their decision-making. This was the most important factor, selected by nine in ten (89%).
Reputation, price, specialism and speed remain key factors, as seen in previous years.
This emerged as the most important factor (89%) this year that consumers would consider if they could shop around, with reputation and price also remaining important.

kp.k: Confidence was high, with weaker results for vulnerable groups
kp.d: The report states that 95% were confident their provider would deliver good service, versus 93% in 2024. Confidence was lower among young adults, Asian respondents, tenants with housing issues, immigration-service users and benefits or tax-credit users, and among those perceiving limited choice (77%, versus 96% among those perceiving choice). The subgroup text uses a conflicting overall comparator of 92%. Separately, 92% trusted their provider to keep their money safe, broadly stable against 2022–2024.
qs: Almost all consumers were confident in the choice they made (95%), in line with high levels seen in 2024 (93%).
18 to 24 year olds (84% vs. 92% overall);
Those who felt that they had limited choice in their provider (77% vs. 96% of those who felt they had a choice).
92% of respondents were confident that the legal service provider they used would keep their money safe, a similar proportion to that reported in 2024 (91%), 2023 (90%) and 2022 (91%).

kp.k: Value-for-money perceptions improved, but limited choice correlated negatively
kp.d: Some 73% rated service and advice good or very good value, compared with 70% in 2024; the report calls this a significant increase and the highest result since 2012. Ratings were higher among employment-dispute users (81%) and will-writing users (78%). They were lower among Asian respondents (68%), South East residents (67%), consumers perceiving limited choice (35%), and those wanting to shop around but not knowing how (53%).
qs: This is a significant increase from last year, and the highest level seen since the survey began in 2012 (see Figure 6).
Those using will writing services (78%) or seeking help with employment disputes (81%).
Those who felt their choice was limited (35%) or wanted to shop around but didn’t know how (53%).

kp.k: Direct discussion remains the main route to price information
kp.d: Discussion with the provider was how 60% first learned the price, stable over three years. Figure 8 reports 10% first found prices on the provider’s website, 8% upon receiving the bill, 7% in an advertisement and 7% on a comparison website. Direct discussion was particularly common among consumers aged 55+ (72%) and users of conveyancing, will-writing, power-of-attorney and document-certification services.
qs: Having a discussion with the provider remained the most common way that consumers found out about the price of legal services (60%), remaining stable over the last three years (see Figure 8).
How did you FIRST find out what the price of the service would be?

kp.k: Price comprehension and comparison remain broadly stable
kp.d: Some 77% found price information easy to understand, generally consistent with results since 2018. Difficulty was higher among minority ethnic communities (8%) and users with landlord (13%) or tenant (8%) housing problems. Among respondents comparing more than one legal service, 69% found price comparisons easy, consistent with 2024 and above 2018–2021 levels. This was easier for White respondents (72%) than minority ethnic respondents (65%), and for will-writing users (76%).
qs: Three quarters of consumers (77%) found it easy to understand the cost of their legal services. This is generally in line with levels seen since 2018.
69% of consumers found price comparisons easy this year, consistent with 2024 but higher than reported between 2018 and 2021.
Those from White backgrounds (72% vs. 65% of those from minority ethnic communities);
Respondents who compared more than one legal service.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: The document contains no concrete claims or predictions about AI changing legal services.
pts.d: The LSCP reports consumer experiences of choosing legal services, comparing providers, understanding prices and assessing value for money. It does not discuss AI or attribute observed market changes to AI. References to online services and independent verification of service quality are not claims about AI or human checking of AI output.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: No evidence is offered for an AI-related claim.
pts.d: The report draws on a survey of 3,750 legal services users, but presents that evidence solely in relation to consumer choice and experience, not AI adoption or effects.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: No AI-related timeframe or conditions are stated.
pts.d: The survey was conducted from 20 February to 7 April 2025 among people who had used legal services in the preceding two years. These dates describe the consumer research, not a timeframe for AI-driven change.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: No group is identified as affected by AI.
pts.d: The research concerns legal services consumers in England and Wales and differences across demographic groups and types of legal need. It does not identify AI-related effects on those consumers, providers, professional roles or the public.
